title: Republic of the Philippines v. Pimentel (2008)
summary: The interpleader could not proceed in a way that adjudicated assets claimed by absent sovereign entities entitled to immunity.
notes:
This is a conjunction of Rule 19, interpleader, and sovereign immunity. It does not establish that every absent claimant requires dismissal in an ordinary private interpleader.

The fund was a Merrill Lynch brokerage account (roughly $35 million) held by Arelma, S.A., a Panamanian company Marcos created; the Pimentel class of human-rights victims held a nearly $2 billion judgment against the Marcos estate and sought to attach the account, and Merrill Lynch filed the statutory interpleader naming the Republic, its Presidential Commission on Good Government, Arelma, PNB and the class.

Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court, reversing the Ninth Circuit, and Justices Stevens and Souter each concurred in part and dissented in part, preferring a remand rather than outright dismissal; the Court held that where a sovereign has a non-frivolous claim to the assets and sovereign immunity, dismissal is required under Rule 19(b) even though the claimants may be left without a forum.

sections.Parties: A financial institution held assets claimed both by victims holding a judgment against the Marcos estate and by the Republic of the Philippines and its commission.
sections.Material Facts: The disputed assets were associated with an entity connected to Marcos. The Republic and its commission claimed that the assets belonged to the Philippines because they were derived from wrongdoing. They invoked sovereign immunity. The competing judgment creditors sought distribution of the fund to satisfy their judgment. Resolving entitlement without the sovereigns could impair their asserted ownership.
sections.Procedural History: The lower courts allowed the interpleader to proceed without the sovereign entities. The Supreme Court held that dismissal was required under the Rule 19 analysis.
sections.Issue: Could the action proceed without immune sovereign claimants whose asserted property rights would be affected?
sections.Holding: No in these circumstances. Their immunity and substantial claims weighed strongly against adjudication in their absence.
sections.Reasoning: The Court required respect for the sovereign interest without deciding its ultimate merits merely to justify proceeding. A court cannot acknowledge immunity and then effectively resolve the immune party’s property claim against it. The analysis remained practical under Rule 19(b), but immunity gave the absent interests unusual force. The possible lack of an immediate alternative remedy for the judgment creditors did not overcome the prejudice to the sovereigns. In considering the adequacy of another remedy, the identity of the stakeholder plaintiff also mattered.

learning.why: The interpleader could not proceed in a way that adjudicated assets claimed by absent sovereign entities entitled to immunity.

topics.cp-required-joinder: The absent sovereign’s substantial property interest required serious consideration under Rule 19.
topics.cp-sovereign-immunity: Immunity prevented joinder and gave special weight to the sovereign’s claim to the assets.
topics.cp-interpleader: Even a useful stakeholder proceeding may have to be dismissed because a required claimant cannot be joined.
topics.cp-frcp-19: The Court applied the four Rule 19(b) factors and held that the sovereign's immunity and non-frivolous claim required dismissal.
topics.cp-nonparty-protection: The decision protects an absent sovereign's interest in its claimed assets even at the cost of leaving the claimants without a forum.
